items.title: L2: Why an up-to-date profile matters
items.source: Civil Service Jobs website; GOV.UK, Working for the Civil Service
items.body: Your Civil Service Jobs profile is the base for every application you make. You fill in your details once and they carry over to each new application, which saves time. This only helps if the details are right. If your email address or phone number has changed and you do not update it, messages about tests and interviews will go to the wrong place. Recruiters often give only a few days to reply to an invitation, so a missed message can end your application. The profile also holds details that departments use when they check eligibility, such as your nationality and whether you have any restrictions on your right to work. Answer these questions truthfully. If your circumstances change, for example you move house or get a new number, update the profile straight away. You can also keep the site helpful by removing alerts you no longer want, so that your inbox does not fill with vacancies that do not suit you. Many people also create a separate email address just for job hunting. This keeps job messages in one place and makes them easy to find. Choose a sensible, professional address, because recruiters will see it. Check this inbox at least once a day while you have live applications.

items.title: L2: Searching smartly and managing alerts
items.body: Searching well saves time and means you find more of the jobs that suit you. Start with a broad keyword such as administration, customer service or casework. Many entry-level jobs have different titles in different departments, so do not rely on one word. Then use filters to narrow the results. Location is useful, but check whether the role can be done in more than one place, since some adverts list several offices. Grade is one of the best filters for finding entry-level jobs, because it lets you see Administrative Officer or Administrative Assistant roles. Working pattern lets you find part-time or flexible roles. After you find a useful set of filters, save the search and turn on an alert. Alerts can often be set to arrive straight away or in a regular summary, depending on the options offered. When a vacancy appears, open it quickly and read the closing date first. Some vacancies close early if a large number of applications arrive, and the advert may say so. Bookmark adverts you plan to apply for and note the reference. Remember that the site may show vacancies from many departments in the same list, so read the department name carefully before you decide.

items.title: L2: How an advert is laid out
items.body: Most Civil Service adverts follow a similar layout, so once you have read one it is easier to read others. At the top are the job title, department, grade, location, salary and closing date. Below these come the working pattern and the type of contract, such as permanent or fixed term. A summary of the job explains what the team does. A list of responsibilities describes the day-to-day tasks. For an Administrative Officer these may include handling post and email, keeping records, answering enquiries and updating computer systems. The person specification, sometimes called the essential criteria, lists what the successful person must show. A section called benefits sets out things such as annual leave, the Civil Service pension and flexible working. Another section describes how to apply and what the selection process will be. It includes the stages and sometimes the dates for sift, tests and interview. The advert also states who is eligible, for example the nationality rules, and the level of security checks required. At the end there is usually a contact for questions and for reasonable adjustments. A fixed-term contract has an end date. A permanent contract does not have a set end date. Read the whole advert before you decide to apply.

items.title: L2: Essential and desirable criteria in practice
items.source: Civil Service Jobs adverts; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Essential criteria are the minimum you must show to be considered. If you cannot meet one, your application will normally be sifted out, however good the rest is. For an entry-level role, essential criteria might include the right to work in the UK, good written and spoken English, basic computer skills and the ability to work accurately with detail. Some adverts ask for GCSE-level English and maths, but many do not, so check each one. Desirable criteria are extra. They may be used to choose between candidates who all meet the essential criteria, or they may not be scored at all. The advert will say how they are used. To show that you meet a criterion, give a specific example from paid work, unpaid work, study or home life. Say what you did and what happened. A claim such as I am good with computers is weak. A claim such as I use spreadsheets to keep a weekly record of household costs and check the totals is stronger because it gives detail. Do not claim experience you do not have. Assessors can ask follow-up questions. If you meet nearly all the criteria but one, think carefully. If it is essential, applying may not be worthwhile. If it is desirable, you can still apply.

items.title: L2: Success Profiles in an advert
items.body: Success Profiles is the framework the Civil Service uses to describe a job and to choose the right person. It has five elements. Behaviours are the actions and activities a person does that show how they work. Strengths are the things a person does well and enjoys, which give them energy. Ability is the aptitude or potential to do the job, often measured with tests. Technical means the specific professional skills or qualifications needed. Experience is the knowledge and background gained in earlier activities, whether paid or unpaid. A job uses some of the five, and not always all of them. The advert tells you which ones apply and how each will be assessed. For example, an entry-level Administrative Officer advert might assess Behaviours with a written statement, Ability with online tests and Strengths at interview. Technical is often not needed at entry level. It is more common in specialist jobs, such as roles needing a legal or accounting qualification. The aim of Success Profiles is to look at more than a CV, so that people from many backgrounds can show what they can do. Read the advert for the element names, then prepare an example for each. Ask yourself which examples you can use more than once and which must be different.

items.title: L2: The Civil Service Behaviours at entry level
items.body: There are nine Civil Service Behaviours: Seeing the Big Picture, Changing and Improving, Making Effective Decisions, Leadership, Communicating and Influencing, Working Together, Developing Self and Others, Managing a Quality Service and Delivering at Pace. Each behaviour is described at several levels, from the entry grades up to the Senior Civil Service. An advert for an Administrative Officer role usually lists only a few of them, often with a note of the level. For these grades the descriptions are about everyday things. Communicating and Influencing includes listening, being clear and polite, and writing in plain English. Working Together includes helping colleagues, sharing information and respecting different views. Delivering at Pace includes planning your work, meeting deadlines and asking for help when you are behind. Managing a Quality Service includes following procedures accurately, checking your own work and treating customers fairly. Making Effective Decisions includes using the information you have and asking when you are not sure. Changing and Improving includes spotting small ways to do a job better. Developing Self and Others includes learning from feedback and helping people who are new. Read the behaviours named in your advert and learn what each means at your level. Then think of two or three real examples for each.

items.title: L2: What happens at the sift
items.source: Civil Service Recruitment Principles; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: The sift is the first big filter in a Civil Service recruitment. Recruiters read the applications and score them against the criteria in the advert. A common method is that every application is read against the same marking guide. Some roles ask for a personal statement. Others ask for written answers to a few questions about behaviours. Some use a short application form where you describe your experience. In larger campaigns a sift may also use a scored multiple-choice test, and a high number of applicants can lead to a high pass mark. The sift usually has a pass mark, and only candidates who reach it move on. If many people reach the mark, the department may apply a higher one so that the number fits the places available for the next stage. This means a good answer may still be sifted out in a very competitive campaign. It also means that it is worth applying again if you are unsuccessful. Sift decisions are made on the information in your application, so the best way to do well is to give clear, specific, honest evidence for each criterion. Departments often tell candidates the sift result by email, and you can ask for feedback. Assessors may look at your evidence for each criterion separately.

items.title: L2: Taking online tests
items.source: Civil Service Jobs; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Many entry-level Civil Service campaigns use online tests, usually multiple choice and against the clock. Typical tests include verbal reasoning, numerical reasoning and situational judgement. You are normally sent an invitation by email with a link, a deadline and details of the time allowed. Read the invitation carefully. Find out whether you can pause, whether a calculator and paper are allowed, and which device and browser to use. Take the test in a quiet place with a good internet connection, and close other programmes so nothing interrupts you. Practise first. Many websites and the Civil Service itself provide sample tests, and practice helps you understand the format and timing. Do not use someone else to take the test for you. Some tests are checked by a second short test or by a questionnaire at interview, so cheating is easy to spot and can end an application. If you have a disability or health condition, ask for reasonable adjustments, such as extra time, before you start the test. Keep an eye on the time but do not rush the first questions. If you are stuck on one question, make your best guess and move on, since every question usually carries the same mark. Afterwards, wait for the department to tell you the result.

items.title: L2: Interview basics and the STAR method
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Most Civil Service interviews are held by a small panel, usually two or three people, who ask the same questions of every candidate so that the process is fair. They are often held by video. One person leads and the others take notes and score your answers against the criteria. Questions are usually about behaviours and strengths. A behaviour question asks for an example of something you did, such as a time you helped a colleague meet a deadline. A strengths question is shorter and asks what you enjoy and do well. STAR is a simple way to structure an example. Situation is where you set the scene briefly. Task is what you were responsible for. Action is what you personally did, step by step. Result is what happened and what you learned. Spend most of your answer on the Action. Say I rather than we, because the panel is scoring you, not the group. Use real detail, such as numbers and outcomes. If a question is unclear, ask politely for it to be repeated. It is fine to take a moment to think. Prepare your examples in advance by writing short notes, but do not learn a script. Try the video call in advance to test your camera and sound.

items.title: L2: Checks, nationality and right to work
items.source: Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Every Civil Service job offer depends on pre-employment checks. The minimum set is the Baseline Personnel Security Standard, or BPSS. It confirms your identity, your nationality and right to work in the UK, your employment history and any unspent criminal convictions. The employment history usually covers the past three years. You will be asked for original documents and for the details of previous employers or other people who can confirm what you were doing. If you were not working, for example because you were caring for children, you will be asked to explain how you spent the time and may need someone who can confirm it. Honesty is essential. Leaving something out or giving wrong information can lead to an offer being withdrawn, even if the original fact would not have mattered. Nationality rules decide which jobs you can do. Many jobs are open to UK nationals and also to citizens of some other countries and people with certain immigration permissions. Some jobs, such as those involving national security, are reserved for UK nationals only. Each advert has an eligibility statement saying who can apply. Read it before you apply, and use the contact in the advert if you are unsure. Do not assume your situation is the same as someone else's.

items.title: L2: Fair and open recruitment
items.body: The Recruitment Principles are the rules that govern how people are appointed to the Civil Service. They are published by the Civil Service Commission, which is independent of the government of the day. The Commission was put on a legal footing by the Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010. Two main ideas stand behind the rules. First, appointments are made on merit, which means the person best able to do the job is chosen after assessment against the criteria. Second, appointments are made after fair and open competition, which means vacancies are advertised and everyone eligible has a chance to apply. There are some exceptions, such as short-term appointments or placements for people with specific needs, but the general rule is open competition. Departments must keep records of how they made their decisions, so that decisions can be checked. They must also treat candidates fairly and avoid discrimination under the Equality Act 2010. If you believe the rules were not followed, first complain to the department using its complaints process. If you are not satisfied with the reply, you can ask the Civil Service Commission to look at whether the Recruitment Principles were breached. The Commission can look at a complaint only about the process, not about whether you should have been given the job.

items.title: L2: Disability Confident and adjustments in practice
items.source: Disability Confident scheme, GOV.UK; Equality Act 2010
items.body: The Civil Service takes part in the Disability Confident scheme. The scheme has three levels: Committed, Employer and Leader. The Civil Service has a guaranteed interview commitment: a disabled applicant who meets the minimum criteria for the role is offered an interview. The minimum criteria are the essential requirements in the advert. To use the commitment you usually tick a box on the application or tell the department that you wish to be considered under the scheme. The Equality Act 2010 defines a disabled person as someone with a physical or mental impairment that has a substantial and long-term negative effect on their ability to do normal daily activities. Many conditions can count, including dyslexia, diabetes, epilepsy, depression and autism. You do not need to have a formal label. If you are unsure whether you count, you can ask the department. Reasonable adjustments are changes that remove a disadvantage. In recruitment these include extra time in tests, accessible formats, a different interview arrangement or a break. The department decides what is reasonable, but it must consider your request properly. What is reasonable depends on the cost, the practicality and the effect on the person. Information you give about a disability is used to make adjustments and is treated as confidential.
